archetype.name: Pocket Passer (timing and accuracy)
archetype.definition: Burrow wins from the pocket with anticipation and ball placement, getting the ball out on time and finishing near the top of the league in completion percentage over expected rather than creating with his legs.

report.headline: The intermediate game is carrying him; the short game is dragging him down.
report.take:
Burrow is what he has been for most of his career: an accuracy-first pocket passer running the most pass-heavy offense in football. Cincinnati leads the league in pass rate over expected (+6.9 in neutral states), and he turns that into 272.2 yards a game (7th) with a 71.4% completion rate (4th) and +5.35 CPOE. That CPOE fits his history. He ranked 1st in 2021, 3rd in 2024 and 10th last year, so the accuracy is not a hot streak.

The season has two halves. Weeks 1 and 2 produced negative passing EPA both times, and the Houston game was the low point: five sacks, 30.6% of dropbacks pressured and a 19.4% bad-throw rate. Since then he has been a different quarterback. Over the last three games he is at 0.286 EPA per dropback with a 9.0 CPOE and a 2.4% sack rate, despite a 1-2 record in those games. Almost all of the value comes on throws of 10+ air yards: 1.093 EPA per attempt on 58 throws, adding up to 63.4 EPA. That is more than double his entire dropback total of 30. The intermediate window is the engine: 43 attempts, 0.939 EPA per play, 74.4% success and a 17.2 CPOE. Tee Higgins (0.583 EPA per target) and Ja'Marr Chase (0.475) are winning there, and Mike Gesicki has been very efficient on a smaller sample.

The averages hide a drag underneath. Throws under 10 air yards are at -0.154 EPA per play and cost him 20.1 points. The 31 throws behind the line of scrimmage are at -0.489 per play, and Chase Brown's 28 targets have cost 11 points. Burrow is also playing more conservatively. His aggressiveness is down to 13.76% from 17.4%, his time to throw has dropped to 2.57 seconds from 2.8, and he throws 1.3 yards short of the sticks on average. The quick release explains his best number, a 20% pressure-to-sack rate (8th), which is far better than the roughly 30% he has posted in recent seasons. His bad-throw rate jumped 7.7 points from last year, which looks alarming. The career line says otherwise: 12.7% sits right in his normal 10-14% band, and last season's 5.0% was the outlier.

Going forward, the volume is safe. The offense passes by design, and a defense that ranks 28th against the run will keep games competitive. The efficiency should settle between the shaky start and the recent peak. Four touchdowns on 15 deep attempts will not hold, but the intermediate accuracy is a skill he has shown for years. If the staff trims the screens and RB checkdowns, there is room for this to become a top-five efficiency season.

strengths.title: Intermediate accuracy drives everything
strengths.body: On throws of 10-19 air yards he completes 74.4% with a 17.2 CPOE and 0.939 EPA per play. This is the core of his game, and it matches the CPOE ranks he has posted across his career. Higgins and Chase are winning outside and over the middle, so expect this to hold even as the per-play figure cools.

strengths.title: Quick release keeps sacks down
strengths.body: He is getting the ball out in 2.57 seconds, down from 2.8 last year. Only 20% of his pressures have become sacks (8th), against a career norm near 30%. That matters behind a line that ranks 25th in hit rate allowed. The timing change is real, but part of the sack avoidance will probably drift back toward his history.

strengths.title: Hot form since Week 3
strengths.body: Over the last three games he is at 0.286 EPA per dropback and a 9.0 CPOE, both well above his season marks. That stretch included Pittsburgh, the 6th-ranked defense, where he posted 14.7 EPA. The rough opening two weeks look more like a slow start than the real level.

concerns.title: Short game and screens bleed points
concerns.body: Throws under 10 air yards are at -0.154 EPA per play, and passes behind the line are at -0.489 with only 19.4% success. Chase Brown's targets alone have cost 11 points. This is mostly a play-calling and personnel problem rather than a Burrow flaw, since his short CPOE is near neutral. It will keep capping his efficiency until the staff leans on it less.

concerns.title: Deep touchdown rate will cool
concerns.body: He has 4 touchdowns and 1.537 EPA per play on just 15 deep attempts, with a 22 CPOE. That is a small-sample spike, especially since he has thrown deep sparingly for years. Expect the deep efficiency, and some of the touchdown pace, to come down.

concerns.title: Protection still cracks
concerns.body: He is hit or sacked on 18.2% of dropbacks, and the offense ranks 25th in hit rate allowed. Houston showed the downside: five sacks and a 19.4% bad-throw rate in Week 2. The quick game is masking a real line issue rather than fixing it.

trend.note: Negative passing EPA in Weeks 1 and 2 gave way to 14.7, 7.4 and 13.9 over the next three games, with his sack rate falling sharply. The team went 1-2 in that stretch anyway, which reflects a leaky run defense more than his play.

nextGame.headline: Baltimore's soft deep coverage meets Burrow's best throws; checkdowns won't work.
nextGame.body:
Baltimore's pass defense is split in a way that matches Burrow's own split. It ranks 4th against short throws (-0.154 EPA) but 22nd against deep ones (0.651), and it has allowed 0.64 EPA per target to opposing WR1s, 31st in the league. It also funnels targets to receivers: 64.2% of throws against it go to WRs, versus a 58.6% league share. Its RB1 and TE1 coverage ranks 2nd and 5th. If Cincinnati leans on Higgins and Chase at 10+ yards, Burrow should be efficient. If the game plan drifts back to screens and Brown checkdowns, it plays straight into Baltimore's strength. Their 9th-ranked hit rate means the quick release matters again.

The Bengals are 2.5-point underdogs coming off a bye with a 51.5 total. Lamar Jackson is listed out with an ankle sprain but is described as day-to-day and could practice. If he plays, Baltimore's 6th-ranked passing offense should push this toward a shootout and more volume for Burrow. Center Cam Jurgens is out, which dents Baltimore's offense either way. On Cincinnati's side, backup TE Tanner Hudson's move to IR barely changes anything. Burrow's own Week 2 questionable tag is stale, and he is listed active.

keyMatchups.title: Higgins and Chase versus soft outside coverage
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore allows the second-most EPA per target to WR1s and ranks 22nd against deep throws. Burrow's 10+ air-yard game is where nearly all his value lives, so this is the matchup that decides his day.

keyMatchups.title: Short area is closed
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore ranks 4th against short passes and 2nd against lead backs. Burrow's under-10 game is already negative, so every screen or Brown checkdown here is likely a wasted down.

keyMatchups.title: Lamar's status sets the script
keyMatchups.body: With Jackson, Baltimore's pass offense ranks 6th, and Cincinnati's defense is 28th against the run, so the Bengals will likely need to keep throwing. A healthy Jackson points to a high-volume afternoon. Without him, Burrow may face a more conservative, lower-scoring game.

nextGame.watch: How many of his throws travel 10+ air yards versus how many go to Chase Brown behind the line.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume is the sturdiest part of the outlook. Cincinnati passes more than any team in neutral situations, and a run defense this leaky keeps the ball in his hands late. Expect yards to stay in the top ten, around 250-295 a game. The efficiency should land between his ugly first two weeks and his hot last three. The intermediate accuracy is a career-long skill and will hold. The 4-for-15 deep touchdown line and the career-best sack avoidance are the pieces most likely to give some back.

The upside case is a schematic one. If the staff cuts the behind-the-line and RB targets that have cost him roughly a third as many points as his deep and intermediate throws have added, his per-dropback efficiency could stay near 0.20. The downside case is the line. Another Houston-style game is possible behind a unit that allows hits at a bottom-eight rate.
swingFactors: How much the offense leans on screens and RB checkdowns
Pass protection holding up against good rushes

confidence.note: Five games and a 15-attempt deep sample, but a long career baseline supports the accuracy and volume.
